entries.title: 13. Lattice Duality: When counting one way is hard, count the other way
entries.snippet: A 1982 competition problem asks for an infinite weighted sum over all plane points, where each weight is a Gaussian times the count of latti…
entries.text: 13. lattice duality: when counting one way is hard, count the other way a 1982 competition problem asks for an infinite weighted sum over all plane points, where each weight is a gaussian times the count of lattice points inside a circle through that point. the breakthrough: flip the counting order. instead of asking how many lattice points are in each circle, ask which circles contain each lattice point. the discontinuous step function becomes a smooth polar integral, yielding the closed form pi(2g-1)^2 where g = sum e^{-k^2}. \sum_{(x,y)} a(x,y) e^{-(x^2+y^2)} = \pi \left( \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} e^{-k^2} \cdot 2 - 1 \right)^2 = \pi(2g-1)^2

entries.title: 14. Peptide Sequencing: From mass spectrum to protein identity
entries.snippet: Computational proteomics identifies proteins by matching experimental mass spectra against theoretical databases. A peptide fragments along …
entries.text: 14. peptide sequencing: from mass spectrum to protein identity computational proteomics identifies proteins by matching experimental mass spectra against theoretical databases. a peptide fragments along its backbone (cid), producing b/y ions whose mass differences reveal the sequence. the peptide spectrum match (psm) score = -10*log10(p) quantifies confidence that the match is not random. this bridges physics (collision-induced dissociation), computation (database search), and statistics (hypothesis testing). \text{psm score} = -10 \log_{10}(p), \quad p = p(\text{random match} | \text{null hypothesis})

entries.title: 15. Lean, AlphaProof & the Riemann Zero-Free Region
entries.snippet: Formal interactive theorem proving (Lean 4) pairs a small deterministic proof kernel with a stochastic LLM token predictor. The LLM proposes…
entries.text: 15. lean, alphaproof & the riemann zero-free region formal interactive theorem proving (lean 4) pairs a small deterministic proof kernel with a stochastic llm token predictor. the llm proposes tactics as text; the kernel compiles each step against hard-coded rules of inference and returns true/false. alphaproof treats the kernel as a deterministic reward function and self-plays, generating and verifying proofs without human data. the card's theorem — a zero-free region for the riemann zeta function at re(s) >= 7/8 with im(s) != 0 — is the kind of statement mathlib and the tao/kontorovich pnt_plus project formalize. if it compiles, it is 100% correct; no human review required. \zeta(s) \neq 0 \quad \text{for } \re(s) \geq \tfrac{7}{8},\ \im(s) \neq 0

entries.title: 16. The √X Theta-Lift Chain: RH via Automorphic Multiplicity
entries.snippet: The Riemann Hypothesis is the optimal-control problem on the count of primes of a given size. Factored through the Chebyshev function ψ(X) =…
entries.text: 16. the √x theta-lift chain: rh via automorphic multiplicity the riemann hypothesis is the optimal-control problem on the count of primes of a given size. factored through the chebyshev function ψ(x) = σ_{n≤x} λ(n) (the von mangoldt sum), the prime number theorem is ψ(x) ~ x (hadamard / de la vallée-poussin, 1896), and rh is the stronger bound ψ(x) = x + o(x^{1/2} log² x) — the √x is exactly the rh content. in a function-field analogue, stepanov's argument resolves rh using a divisor carrying multiplicity; over the integers, multiplicity is hard to find (“differentiating whole numbers”). the 2026 announcement reports a proof, discovered with claude, that ports stepanov's multiplicity natively into the automorphic setting by chaining theta lifts u(x₀) → u(x₁) → ⋯ → u(x_m) between totally definite unitary groups, each lift raising the multiplicity by one. the chain length is m = √x — the only length that collapses the error into the rh band. the argument is fully formalized in lean (14 tarball parts); the grh extension follows, and the extended rh is expected with more time. \psi(x) := \sum_{n \leq x} \lambda(n) = x + o\!\left(x^{1/2}\log^2 x\right) \;\longleftrightarrow\; \text{rh}
